title: Product photography for a furniture maker
excerpt: Photograph furniture for scale and material, in one setting, with dimensions left in text. Mixed rooms make the workshop look unfinished.
alt: Two white smartwatch mockups on a plain light background, one showing the face and one the back. Furniture photos need that pair: the whole piece and the material, on one ground.
caption: Face and back, one background. The catalog needs the same pair. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How do you show the size of a chair in a photograph?
faqs.answer: Show the whole piece with a repeatable scale cue, such as a standing person used the same way each time, and publish dimensions in text. Keep the camera level and far enough back that a wide lens does not bend the legs. The picture will be believed before the numbers, so it must not fight them.

faqs.question: What should stay out of the image file?
faqs.answer: Prices, lead times, and slogans. Those change, and they are hard to read as text. Alt text can describe the piece and the view. The lead time stays a sentence a person can edit when the workshop changes.

faqs.question: When should you reshoot?
faqs.answer: When the finish changes, when the prototype still has marks you would not ship, or when one hero was shot in a different room or a different sky. A half-updated grid looks unfinished. Hold the old system until you can move the whole catalog.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A furniture maker product photography practice shows scale, material, and the piece as it will occupy a room, with one crop and one kind of light across the catalog. Lead time will not appear in the file. It must not be contradicted by a file that looks like a warehouse ready to ship tomorrow if the chair takes ten weeks. Mixed crops make the workshop look unfinished.

Photograph the whole piece first. Let details of grain and cloth come second. Hold the background still so the grid reads as one maker.

## The set that answers size and material

Each piece needs a small, repeatable set.

- A full piece, in the shared setting, with margin around it so the silhouette survives a thumbnail.
- A second full view from the angle that explains the form: side of a chair, back of a shelf, open door of a cabinet.
- A material detail: grain, join, weave, or edge, in the same light.
- A scale cue that is consistent: a person standing beside it, or a known table height, not a different trick every time.

Dimensions still live in text on the page. The photograph will be believed first, so it must not fight the numbers. A wide lens close to a sofa makes it longer than the inches you publish. Step back, keep the camera level, and use a normal perspective. Architectural drama that bends the legs will become a complaint when the real piece has straight legs.

If a person is the scale cue, use the same approach every time: standing, full height in frame, plain clothing. A seated person is a second system, useful for chairs, and then you use it for chairs, not for one chair. Say their height in the caption or the page if the cue would otherwise lie. Children in the frame change the scale story. Avoid them unless the piece is for children and you are consistent.

The detail frame is where cheap photography flatters or insults the work. Get close enough to see the grain. Do not get so close that a small repair or a knot becomes the whole product. The detail supports the full piece. It does not replace it in the grid.

## One room, or one sweep

Choose the setting and stay. A corner of the workshop with a concrete floor, a single rented room with one window, or a plain sweep. The catalog should feel like one place. A beach house, a white box, and a café in the same collection is the mixed look, and buyers will trust the work less because the pictures do not agree with each other.

Light follows the place. Window light can be the system if you shoot at the same time of day and you control the bounce. Mixed flash and mixed windows across a month will make identical ash look like two woods. When you cannot repeat the light, do not add the new frame to the grid until you can.

Reflections in finishes are part of the material. A gloss that you polarize into looking like matte is a different product. Show the finish you sell. If you sell both, they are two frames, labeled.

Props must be quieter than the furniture. A single book, a lamp you also sell, or nothing. A styled room that hides the legs with a throw has failed, because the legs are often the design. If you sell the throw, it can appear as its own product, not as camouflage.

## Crop, horizon, and the grid

Set the camera height for each type. Tables at a height that shows the top and the leg. Chairs at a height that shows the seat and the back. Shelves tall enough to see the whole case without tilting, because tilt makes the sides diverge and the piece look badly made. Write the heights down. "Eye level" is not a measurement if several people shoot.

Leave a similar margin. The largest piece will fill more of the frame if the distance is constant, which is what you want. Do not zoom the stool until it feels as important as the wardrobe. Importance in the grid should follow size or leave the sizing to the page, but it should not be a random zoom.

Check every hero in the real category template at phone width. A dark wood piece on a dark floor can disappear. Separate them with the background you chose, or light the edge. If one piece vanishes, the grid looks broken. Fix the frame, not the buyer's brightness setting.

Campaign photographs with people living a whole scene can live on the homepage. The thumbnail remains the quiet full piece. When a new series tempts you to change rooms, change all the thumbnails or none. A half-moved catalog is the unfinished shop.

## Weight of the file, and words that do not belong in it

These frames are large, and they are the largest element on the page. Google's [Core Web Vitals](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/core-web-vitals) targets are Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint under 200 milliseconds, and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. Export a size the template actually needs. Reserve the space so the price and the lead time do not jump when the sofa arrives. A jump on a page where the price is high feels like the number changed.

Do not set type in the photograph: prices, lead times, "handmade," arrows pointing at a joint. Lead time changes. The [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) wants the alternative text to describe the picture, and the real information to be text. "Oak dining chair, side view, in a white room" is alt text. The eight-week lead time is a sentence on the page, where a person can update it when the queue changes. Text burned into a JPEG will keep promising the old queue.

Name files by piece, finish, and view. The person updating the shop after a finishing day should not guess which frame is walnut. Wrong finish on the page is a material lie, and it is a photography operations problem as much as a design problem.

Keep the masters. You will recrop when the template changes, and you will need the margin you left. A tight export cannot grow back into an honest full piece.

## What the picture must not promise

If the piece is made to order, do not photograph a stacked warehouse of identical chairs unless that is the truth. A single chair in the real finish is the honest hero. If you have one in the showroom, say it is the showroom piece and the one they buy will be made. Buyers accept that when you say it. They do not accept a scuff they were not shown, so photograph a finished piece, not a prototype with pencil marks, unless you are selling the prototype.

Do not hide a flaw you would disclose in the workshop. Photography that erases a filled knot you would mention in person creates a different contract. Light cosmetic retouch of sensor dust is fine. Rebuilding a joint in software is not.

Do not use a room so luxurious that the price looks like a bargain you cannot explain, or so chaotic that the work looks accidental. The room is a measuring tool. It is not a personality you borrow.

An [intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) can be a review of six heroes on a phone. The question is whether scale and material survive the thumbnail, and whether any frame promises a lead time the workshop does not have.

## Outdoor light and pieces that do not move

If you shoot outside, you are accepting clouds. Schedule the catalog for one kind of day, and stop when the light changes rather than "finishing the list" under a different sky. A chair in sun and a chair in open shade will not sit together. Either wait, or move the second piece indoors into the system you already trust. A deadline is a poor reason to mix them. The grid lasts longer than the afternoon.

Large pieces need a plan for the door and the truck before the camera plan. A wardrobe you cannot get into the chosen room will be shot in a hallway out of necessity, and that hallway will not match the stool you shot last month. Choose the setting that the largest piece can enter, then shoot the small pieces there too. The room follows the biggest object, not the prettiest corner.

Protect the finish from the shoot itself. Sand, grit, and a stand that dents a leg will create damage you then have to retouch or disclose. The photography is not allowed to become a repair. Pads, clean hands, and a person who knows which edge is fragile are part of the setup, as much as the light.

## Direction the bench can keep

Write one page: setting, camera height per type, the frame set, the scale cue, export size, alt pattern, and the rule that lead time and dimensions stay in text. When you add a new type, such as a lamp or a bed, add a row before you shoot. A bed is not a tall chair. Forcing the chair crop onto it will cut the headboard or shrink it into illegibility.

On shoot day, finish one piece's set before you restyle the room. Partial sets are how the detail frame gets forgotten and later shot under a different sky. Mark rejects with a reason: tilted, dark edge, prop on the leg, wide-angle bend. The next session starts from those notes.

When the finish formula changes, reshoot the affected heroes before you publish the new finish name. A new name on an old color is the same mismatch as a mixed crop. The grid should look like the workshop on its best ordinary day, repeated, not like a different studio every month.

Skincare is a smaller object with a stricter claim problem. [An online shop for a skincare brand](/blog/an-online-shop-for-a-skincare-brand) is next, because the page has to show ingredients and restraint rather than a wall of promises, and the photograph will have to do the same.
